title: The last two of al-Baqarah
hook: our Lord, do not burden us beyond what we can bear (2:285–286)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ayat al-Kursi: the Living, the Sustainer, untouched by drowsiness. Your line was he does not sleep.

Have you ever read a rule and felt your stomach drop? Not because you wanted to break it, but because you knew you couldn't keep it. That happened to the companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ near the end of Surah al-Baqarah. A verse came saying that whether you show what's in yourselves or hide it, Allah will bring you to account for it. What's in yourselves: the thoughts you never chose. Sahih Muslim records that they came to the Prophet and fell to their knees: this is more than we can bear. What happened next became the surah's ending, two verses still said at night.
screen: `A VERSE THAT FELT TOO HEAVY.` → `ON THEIR KNEES: MORE THAN WE CAN BEAR.` → `WHAT CAME NEXT.`

segments.voice: The Prophet told them not to turn away but to say: we hear and we obey; Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the return. They said it, and the words came back to them as scripture. Verse two eighty-five describes the messenger and the believers who believe in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers, and who say exactly that. Then verse two eighty-six opens with the answer to their fear. Pickthall: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope. Scope, in Arabic wus', means capacity, width, room. You are asked for what you have room for. Each soul gets what it earned, and bears what it did. Then the verse becomes a list of pleas, the ones the companions made on their knees. Our Lord, don't take us to task if we forget or make mistakes. Don't lay on us a burden like the ones laid on those before us. Don't load us with what we have no strength for. Pardon us, forgive us, have mercy on us. You are our Protector. The report in Sahih Muslim adds that after each plea, Allah answered: I have done so. The worry about unchosen thoughts is answered too: other hadith say a person isn't held to account for passing thoughts they don't act on or speak. And Bukhari records the Prophet saying that whoever recites these last two verses at night, they will be enough for him. A heavy verse, then a gentle ending.
screen: `WE HEAR AND WE OBEY.` · `WUS' — CAPACITY, ROOM.` · `DON'T TAKE US TO TASK IF WE FORGET.` · `I HAVE DONE SO.` · then, large: `NOT BEYOND WHAT WE BEAR.`

segments.voice: Let the pleas of verse two eighty-six pass by, one per breath: with one real slip in mind, don't take us to task if we forget or make mistakes; with one worry, don't load us with what we have no strength for; then pardon, forgiveness, mercy. Rest on the line beneath them all: not beyond its scope. If you pray, you can recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah tonight, or just their pleas.
Wus', capacity: the scope Allah tasks no soul beyond, in the last two verses of al-Baqarah, two eighty-five and six.
Your line: not beyond what we bear. It answered people on their knees. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims recite the last two verses of Surah al-Baqarah (2:285–286) at night before sleep, following the hadith that they suffice whoever recites them; the pleas of 2:286 are also said as a du'a on their own.

original.note: Arabic: Allah tasks no soul except within its capacity (2:286).

trapdoor: what you thought: a promise that life won't be hard.
what it means: each soul is asked only for what it has room for, followed by pleas for pardon, forgiveness and mercy.
what a scholar hears: Muslim 125–126 on the revelation after 2:284; 'I have done so' after each plea; Bukhari 5009, the two verses suffice at night.

chat.says: Does God ask more of people than they can carry?
options: No. The verse says no soul is tasked beyond its capacity, its wus'.
Yes. He holds people to account for every passing thought they never act on.
No, because He asks nothing at all of people who find faith hard.
chat.meaning: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope: wus', capacity, room. You are asked for what you have room for.
